subject: Hybrid ingress design decision: Hub-and-spoke + PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Tessa Morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.com>
To: Kelly Park <kelly@acmecorp.com>, Acme Infra Team <infra@acme.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 19 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Hybrid ingress design decision: Hub-and-spoke + PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN

Hi Kelly / Acme Infra team —

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. As promised, attached is a short decision memo summarizing Redwood's recommended connectivity approach for your Private deployment (VPC + on-prem workloads). High-level ask from Acme: low-latency inference (<30ms p95 for regional requests), strict private data controls (no public internet egress for inference traffic), and phased rollout across three regions with a central management VPC.

Options we evaluated (concise):
- VPC Peering (direct peering between Acme VPCs and Redwood VPCs): lowest latency, but scales poorly across many accounts/regions and complicates egress control.
- AWS PrivateLink (NLB + interface endpoints): strong security boundary (no cross-VPC route tables exposed), better cross-account scaling, explicit endpoint-level IAM controls, modest latency overhead (~5–15ms depending on path).
- Site-to-Site VPN (IPSec): simple to boot, predictable control of on-prem exits, but variable latency and not recommended for production inference at scale unless terminated into a transit gateway with dynamic routing and redundancy.

Recommendation (short): adopt a hybrid hub-and-spoke model using a Transit Gateway in the central account and expose Redwood inference endpoints via PrivateLink interface endpoints per-spoke. Use selective VPC peering only for low-latency internal-only workloads in the same account/zone (e.g., batching/ETL). Reserve S2S VPN for legacy on-prem connectivity and a backup path for failover.

Key tradeoffs we want you to acknowledge before we proceed with a pilot:
1) Latency: PrivateLink adds a small extra hop (NLB -> ENI) — we validated p95 in our benchmarks at ~8–12ms within us-west-2 using our NLB setup. If Acme requires <10ms p95 for every flow, we should scope a colocated cluster in your VPC (peering/transit attachments) instead.
2) Egress & Audit: PrivateLink keeps traffic inside AWS control plane and is easier to audit; peering requires careful route table hygiene to avoid accidental cross-account egress.
3) Operational: Transit Gateway + PrivateLink gives a single place to apply NAT/inspection and scales well across 12+ spokes; peering is simple but brittle at scale.

Attachments: a one-page matrix (connectivity-decision-matrix.xlsx) and a diagram (hub-spoke-privatelink-peering-vpn.png). I'll schedule a 30-min pilot planning call if you agree.

Next steps suggested (pick one):
- Option A: Pilot with Transit Gateway + PrivateLink in us-west-2 (recommended)
- Option B: Pilot with direct peering and a colocated Redwood private cluster in your account (if you prioritize absolute minimal intra-region latency)

Thanks — happy to jump on a call.

—Tessa
Tessa Morgan
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Tessa —

Appreciate the concise memo. A couple quick clarifying questions from our side before we lock a pilot:
1) Can you share the benchmark run parameters that produced the 8–12ms p95 for PrivateLink? Were these small single-token responses or longer streaming workloads?
2) For the Transit Gateway approach, how do you recommend we handle cross-region traffic (we want to avoid inter-region egress charges if possible)?
3) On the security side, we need proof we can produce per-request audit/logging tied to Acme user ids and not just the Redwood service principal — is that supported with PrivateLink?

Also tagging our infra lead Mark (mark@acme.com) who will be on the pilot. We prefer Option A unless the latency profile for streaming generation is significantly worse.

Thanks,
Kelly
Kelly Park
Head of Product, ACME Corp

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Hybrid ingress design decision: Hub-and-spoke + PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN

Folks —

Quick internal note and responses we can send back to Acme:

1) Benchmark details (attach short reproducible script): our 8–12ms p95 numbers were measured with a 256-token prompt, single-request, non-streaming, within us-west-2 across accounts using an NLB-backed PrivateLink. I'll attach the run flags in the sheet and a minimal client script. For streaming, we see an additional ~6–10ms p95 due to connection setup/initial flush; steady-state token latency is comparable.

2) Cross-region: recommend local endpoints in each region and use asynchronous replication for model artifacts. Transit Gateway inter-region peering carries additional charges — better to deploy regional PrivateLink endpoints in each target region. If Acme insists on a central egress point to enforce inspection, we can chain transit attachments but call out cost.

3) Per-request auditability: yes — when using PrivateLink we can require a per-request API key and include Acme tenant id in a custom header that flows through our logs. We can map those to request IDs and export to a customer-owned Kinesis/CloudWatch (or push to a customer-managed S3 bucket via signed role). See attached sample s3-presigned-sample-policy.txt for how to hook logs into a customer bucket with least privilege.

My recommended reply to Kelly: confirm Option A (Transit Gateway + PrivateLink pilot in us-west-2), share benchmark artifacts, and request temporary IAM role + ephemeral account access to create an interface endpoint and test traffic. We should ask for a 2-week pilot window and define explicit SLA/go-no-go latency gates (e.g., p95 < 30ms for non-streaming, and initial token latency p95 < 25ms for streaming start).

—Marcus
Marcus Lin
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
